units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
Surely, Robert! What else is there to do?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: I might see her personally. It would be better.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: You must never see her again, Robert. She is not a woman you should ever speak to. She is not worthy to talk to a man like you. No; you must write to her at once, now, this moment, and let your letter show her that your decision is quite irrevocable!
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Write this moment!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: But it is so late. It is close on twelve.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: That makes no matter. She must know at once that she has been mistaken in you—and that you are not a man to do anything base or underhand or dishonourable. Write here, Robert. Write that you decline to support this scheme of hers, as you hold it to be a dishonest scheme. Yes—write the word dishonest. She knows what that word means.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN sits down and writes a letter .
His wife takes it up and reads it .
Yes; that will do.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Rings bell .
And now the envelope.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: He writes the envelope slowly .
Enter MASON.
Have this letter sent at once to Claridge’s Hotel. There is no answer.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Exit MASON.
LADY CHILTERN kneels down beside her husband , and puts her arms around him .

Robert, love gives one an instinct to things. I feel to-night that I have saved you from something that might have been a danger to you, from something that might have made men honour you less than they do. I don’t think you realise sufficiently, Robert, that you have brought into the political life of our time a nobler atmosphere, a finer attitude towards life, a freer air of purer aims and higher ideals—I know it, and for that I love you, Robert.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Oh, love me always, Gertrude, love me always!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: I will love you always, because you will always be worthy of love. We needs must love the highest when we see it!
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Kisses him and rises and goes out .
SIR ROBERT CHILTERN walks up and down for a moment ; then sits down and buries his face in his hands .
The Servant enters and begins pulling out the lights .
SIR ROBERT CHILTERN looks up .
Put out the lights, Mason, put out the lights!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: The Servant puts out the lights .
The room becomes almost dark .
The only light there is comes from the great chandelier that hangs over the staircase and illumines the tapestry of the Triumph of Love .
Morning-room at Sir Robert Chiltern’s house .
LORD GORING, dressed in the height of fashion , is lounging in an armchair .
SIR ROBERT CHILTERN is standing in front of the fireplace .
He is evidently in a state of great mental excitement and distress .
As the scene progresses he paces nervously up and down the room .

My dear Robert, it’s a very awkward business, very awkward indeed. You should have told your wife the whole thing. Secrets from other people’s wives are a necessary luxury in modern life. So, at least, I am always told at the club by people who are bald enough to know better. But no man should have a secret from his own wife. She invariably finds it out. Women have a wonderful instinct about things. They can discover everything except the obvious.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Arthur, I couldn’t tell my wife. When could I have told her? Not last night. It would have made a life-long separation between us, and I would have lost the love of the one woman in the world I worship, of the only woman who has ever stirred love within me. Last night it would have been quite impossible. She would have turned from me in horror . . . in horror and in contempt.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Is Lady Chiltern as perfect as all that?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes; my wife is as perfect as all that.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Taking off his left-hand glove .
What a pity! I beg your pardon, my dear fellow, I didn’t quite mean that. But if what you tell me is true, I should like to have a serious talk about life with Lady Chiltern.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: It would be quite useless.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: May I try?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes; but nothing could make her alter her views.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Well, at the worst it would simply be a psychological experiment.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: All such experiments are terribly dangerous.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Everything is dangerous, my dear fellow. If it wasn’t so, life wouldn’t be worth living. . . . Well, I am bound to say that I think you should have told her years ago.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: When? When we were engaged? Do you think she would have married me if she had known that the origin of my fortune is such as it is, the basis of my career such as it is, and that I had done a thing that I suppose most men would call shameful and dishonourable?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Slowly .
Yes; most men would call it ugly names. There is no doubt of that.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Bitterly .
Men who every day do something of the same kind themselves. Men who, each one of them, have worse secrets in their own lives.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: That is the reason they are so pleased to find out other people’s secrets. It distracts public attention from their own.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: And, after all, whom did I wrong by what I did? No one.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Looking at him steadily .
Except yourself, Robert.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: After a pause .
